analysis.one_liner: Guarantees every child and pregnant woman enrollment in a qualified health plan.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have entitled every child up to age 22 and every pregnant woman to enrollment in a qualified health plan with no preexisting-condition exclusions, was introduced by Senator Dodd with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and never received any further action before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Public Health Service Act to entitle every child legally residing in the United States, from birth to age 22, and every pregnant woman to enrollment in a qualified health plan through Health Insurance Purchasing Alliances. Plans could not deny or limit coverage based on health status, claims experience, or preexisting conditions, and had to cover preventive care (with no deductible or coinsurance), major medical services, and extended services like mental health, substance abuse treatment, and dental care. Cost sharing was capped: no more than a $200 family deductible, 20-30% coinsurance, and out-of-pocket limits tied to income, with deductibles and coinsurance fully waived for families under 133% of poverty and premium reductions up to 400% of poverty. Medicaid would cover states' shares of premiums, and doctors' boards on health care reform would be required to include pediatric and maternal health representation.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured children and pregnant women, especially in low- and moderate-income families: guaranteed coverage from birth to age 22 with no preexisting-condition exclusions, free preventive care, capped out-of-pocket costs, and free deductibles and coinsurance for families under 133% of poverty. Providers serving uninsured children would be paid as if the patients had been enrolled.

how_it_helps.text: Every legally residing child under 22 and every pregnant woman would be entitled to enrollment in a qualified health plan, with Alliances required to identify and enroll every child in their region by January 1, 1995, and coverage continuous until age 22.
Plans could not deny, limit, or condition coverage of required services based on health status, claims experience, medical history, or preexisting conditions.

Qualified plans had to cover preventive care (immunizations, prenatal care, newborn care, family planning, child abuse assessment, and preventive dental care) with no deductible or coinsurance, plus major medical and extended services including mental health, substance abuse treatment, prescription drugs, and hospice.

Cost sharing was tightly capped: no family deductible over $200, coinsurance no more than 20% for major medical and 30% for extended services, and a cap on total yearly cost sharing at 10% of family income (max $1,000 individual / $3,000 family). Families under 133% of poverty would pay no deductible or coinsurance, and families under 400% of poverty would get premium reductions, with plans compensated for the waivers.

Alliances had to provide outreach services for low-income enrollees, including transportation, child care at service sites, translation, care coordination, and screening follow-ups, and Medicaid would pay states' shares of premiums to enroll children and pregnant women.

analysis.who_pays: Health plans would bear the cost of covering guaranteed high-cost populations (pregnancy, children with preexisting conditions) with premiums capped by Alliances and cost sharing capped by law, compensated for income-based waivers through Medicaid and Alliance payments. States would have to maintain Medicaid spending on children and pay their share of premiums. Families and employers paying Alliance premiums would fund the enrollment base.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health plans, state Medicaid programs, premium payers

drawbacks.text: The bill never specified a dedicated funding source for the expanded coverage beyond state Medicaid premium payments and Alliance premiums, so the cost of enrolling all children and pregnant women, including high-cost cases, would fall on the insurance risk pools and premium payers.

Coverage would run through private qualified health plans and Health Insurance Purchasing Alliances rather than a public program, locking private insurers in as the permanent channel for children's health coverage and adding their overhead to the cost of care.

The bill would preempt any weaker state requirement for coverage of children and pregnant women starting January 1, 1995, and take effect immediately on enactment even before implementing regulations were written, leaving little transition time for plans and Alliances.

Mental health and substance abuse treatment, orthodontia, and therapy services would be subject to higher coinsurance (up to 30%) and a plan-of-care requirement, so families with children needing those services would still face significant costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a broad, concrete benefit: guaranteed, portable coverage for children through age 22 and pregnant women, with the strongest protections aimed at the lowest-income families and the most cost-sensitive services (preventive care) made free. The main honest costs are that it relied on the private insurance and Alliance structure being built by the broader 1993 health reform effort, left open how the expansion would be financed beyond state Medicaid contributions and capped premiums, and layered heavy benefit mandates onto plans whose premiums were regulated. It was a children's and maternal health layer on top of the managed-competition framework, not a stand-alone, self-financing program.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Dodd introduced it on September 14, 1993, the Senate referred it to the Labor and Human Resources Committee, no cosponsors signed on, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Dodd introduced the Children and Pregnant Women Health Insurance Act of 1993 in the Senate on September 14, 1993, and delivered introductory remarks.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources; no cosponsors joined, and that was the last action ever taken on the bill.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 without the committee holding a markup or the Senate ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new benefit from the bill's death. Health plans avoided a mandate to enroll every child and pregnant woman regardless of health status with capped premiums and cost sharing, and children and pregnant women who were uninsured at the time remained so under this bill; children's coverage did not advance until separate legislation years later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health plans; uninsured children stayed uninsured

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks, and referred it to the Labor and Human Resources Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee; no markup, no vote, no further action after the September 14, 1993 referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew opposition on the record: it had no cosponsors, no committee vote, and no floor debate, so no party split ever took shape. It arrived during the larger 1993-94 health care reform fight, in which comprehensive Democratic-led proposals failed in Congress and no Republican alternative advanced (widely reported background).

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would have made private qualified health plans and HMOs the permanent channel for guaranteeing coverage to every child and pregnant woman, with Alliances required to enroll everyone and Medicaid covering premium shares — a large, guaranteed enrollment base. In exchange, plans would have faced a ban on preexisting-condition exclusions, mandated benefit packages, and caps on premiums and cost sharing.

Providers treating unenrolled children or pregnant women would be paid as if the patient had been enrolled, guaranteeing payment for care that often went uncompensated, and health care reform boards would have to include pediatric, obstetric, and maternal health representation.

States would have to maintain their existing level of effort on children's medical services and pay their share of premiums to enroll children and pregnant women in qualified plans, but the federal entitlement would shift much of the coverage burden into the Alliance framework.
